title: What should a Dubai catering venue-access brief include?
body_markdown:
A Dubai catering venue-access brief should identify the delivery entrance, unloading arrangements, staff entry requirements, kitchen facilities, setup window and collection deadline. It should also name the person authorised to resolve access problems. Confirm these details with the venue before finalising the catering plan, because a street address alone does not explain how food, equipment and staff reach the event space.


**TL;DR**

- Catering venue access brief Dubai: confirm entrances, unloading, kitchen access, timings and responsibility before agreeing the event plan.
- Separate venue-confirmed arrangements from requests that still need approval.
- myCHEF suits Dubai households and businesses seeking vetted chefs and event catering; venue arrangements still need explicit agreement.
- Give the venue and caterer the same final brief, including collection and cleaning responsibilities.


For a tailored catering enquiry, [contact myCHEF](https://www.mychef.ae/contact) with your event details and venue-access brief. Use the enquiry to establish the service required and which practical arrangements need confirmation before you agree the scope.

## What should a Dubai catering venue-access brief include?

**Write the brief around the route from arrival to departure, not just the event address.** A caterer needs to understand where the team can enter, what they can use and when everything must leave.

Use this checklist as the structure. Record the venue’s answers rather than assuming that a facility shown during a viewing is included in your booking.

| Brief section | Details to record | Confirmation needed from |
|---|---|---|
| Event identity | Date, venue address, room or villa identifier, guest count and service format | Event organiser |
| Delivery route | Correct entrance, unloading point, route to the service area and any stairs | Venue contact |
| Staff access | Entry procedure, requested identification and any advance submission process | Venue contact |
| Working facilities | Preparation space, cooking equipment, refrigeration, water and washing facilities | Venue and caterer |
| Equipment movement | Lift access, doorway restrictions, trolley route and storage area | Venue contact |
| Timing | Delivery, setup, service, clearing and collection windows | Venue and caterer |
| Responsibilities | Equipment, staffing, rubbish removal, cleaning and final handover | Organiser, venue and caterer |
| Decision contacts | Named organiser, venue representative and catering lead | Each responsible party |

Keep unresolved points visible. A blank field can look like an omission; a field marked awaiting venue confirmation tells everyone that a decision is still outstanding.

## Why does the access brief matter before you agree the menu?

The menu and the venue’s working conditions need to fit together. A dish requiring cooking at the venue needs a different arrangement from food delivered ready for service, while a plated dinner needs a clear route between preparation and guests.

**Confirm the working environment before treating a menu proposal as the final event plan.** Otherwise, the proposal and the venue booking can describe different assumptions about equipment, staffing and preparation.

Keep dietary requirements in the catering brief, too. Identify allergies and other requirements clearly, then ask the caterer what preparation arrangements are needed; do not assume that access to a shared kitchen settles those questions.

## Which entrance and unloading details should you check?

Give the delivery team an arrival instruction that works independently of a guest invitation. A reception entrance, residential lobby or visitor car park is not automatically the agreed route for catering deliveries.

Ask the venue to confirm:

- **Arrival point:** the entrance the catering team should actually use.
- **Unloading:** where the vehicle can stop and who controls that space.
- **Internal route:** the path from unloading to the kitchen or service area.
- **Obstacles:** steps, narrow doors, thresholds or areas unavailable during guest arrival.
- **Parking:** where the driver should go once unloading is complete.
- **Escalation:** whom to call if the agreed entrance is inaccessible.

For a Dubai tower or managed development, ask the building representative about the applicable delivery procedure. For a villa, confirm the gate, parking arrangement and route through the property. These are questions for the specific venue, not assumptions about every Dubai address.

Record directions in words as well as sharing a location pin. A pin identifies a place; it does not explain which gate leads to the working entrance.

## What kitchen and equipment information does the caterer need?

Describe what the team is permitted to use, not simply what exists on site. An appliance in the venue kitchen is only useful to the event plan once access and suitability have been confirmed.

Ask the caterer which photographs or measurements would help assess the space. Useful subjects include the preparation surface, cooking area, refrigeration, washing facilities and the route between kitchen and dining area.

Your brief should distinguish between:

- **Venue equipment:** items the venue has agreed the catering team can use.
- **Caterer equipment:** items included in the agreed catering scope.
- **Separate arrangements:** items another supplier or the organiser must provide.
- **Unresolved items:** anything still awaiting confirmation.

Do not write kitchen available as a substitute for this detail. State whether the agreed use covers preparation, cooking, refrigeration and washing, or only a limited part of the space.

For the related question of who supplies what, the guide to [groceries and equipment for a private chef](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-bring-their-own-groceries-and-equipment) addresses a separate part of the planning conversation. Your event agreement still needs to specify the actual allocation.

## How does the brief change with the service format?

Choose the service format before finalising access arrangements. The following comparison describes planning options, not confirmed packages or inclusions from any individual caterer.

| Service format | Best for | Access advantage | Constraint to resolve |
|---|---|---|---|
| Drop-off catering | Hosts arranging their own food presentation and service | Focuses access planning on delivery and handover | Someone must accept the delivery and manage the agreed next steps |
| Staffed buffet | Events needing an attended serving area | Concentrates service around a defined station | Requires agreed setup space, staff access and clearing arrangements |
| Plated dining | Events built around seated courses | Gives the team a defined service sequence | Requires coordination between preparation, plating and tables |
| Live cooking | Events where cooking forms part of the experience | Places preparation within the planned event setup | Needs explicit venue agreement on equipment, location and working conditions |

Do not choose a format solely because it appears simpler on a menu. Choose the arrangement that fits the space, the guest experience and the responsibilities you want the catering team to take on.

## How should you coordinate the venue and catering timeline?

Build the access plan around the venue’s confirmed working windows. Guest arrival is only one milestone: the team also needs an agreed time to enter, prepare, clear and remove equipment.

Use this sequence when collecting confirmations:

1. **Venue approval:** establish what the venue permits and who can approve changes.
2. **Delivery access:** confirm when food, equipment and staff can enter.
3. **Setup completion:** agree when the working and guest-facing areas must be ready.
4. **Service:** identify the planned start and any event cues affecting food service.
5. **Collection:** confirm when equipment and rubbish must leave, and who signs off the handover.

These stages should appear in the same order in the brief and the event schedule. Keep setup completion distinct from delivery arrival; they describe different points in the work.


![Timeline connecting venue approval, delivery access, setup completion, service and collection](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/72c5b3be-7548-4b33-9cad-5a00653ac05b/body-8f27ac924bcb613a445dbc1267504b1c.jpg)

*Confirm the access sequence as well as the time guests arrive.*


Assign an owner to each milestone. The organiser should not need to guess whether a delayed setup requires a decision from the venue representative, the catering lead or another supplier.

When [sharing the event-day timeline with vendors](https://rundown.pro/blog/how-do-i-share-a-day-of-timeline-with-vendors), connect each catering milestone to the access arrangement it depends on: delivery to unloading, setup to room access, and collection to the final exit window. Send changes to everyone affected, rather than updating only the organiser’s copy.

## Why do venue-access arrangements vary?

The brief changes because the working conditions change. Use these factors to explain the requirements to your caterer, rather than treating every Dubai event space as interchangeable.

- **Property layout:** a ground-level villa and an upper-floor event room need different delivery instructions.
- **Building procedures:** entry approvals and delivery arrangements must come from the relevant venue representative.
- **Service format:** drop-off, staffed service and cooking on site require different working arrangements.
- **Equipment allocation:** borrowed, venue-provided and caterer-supplied items need named responsibility.
- **Event schedule:** guest movements and other suppliers’ work affect when areas can be used.
- **Departure conditions:** collection access and handover requirements shape the end of the service.

These details also belong in the quotation discussion. Ask which access-related work is included and which changes would require a revised scope. Do not assume that equipment movement, extra service responsibilities or a later collection are covered unless the agreement says so.

## Who should confirm the brief before the event?

The organiser should hold the final version, with the venue confirming its own access conditions and the caterer confirming the working plan. Each party should approve the details within its control.

**A message sent is not the same as an arrangement confirmed.** Ask for acknowledgement of the entrance, working window, facilities and departure plan, especially where an earlier version contained unresolved questions.

If the venue changes an access condition, return the change to the catering lead before treating it as settled. A different unloading point or collection window can affect the practical plan even when the guest-facing schedule stays unchanged.

## What should you write if some details are still unknown?

Mark unknown details as awaiting confirmation and assign someone to resolve them. Do not fill gaps with assumptions borrowed from a previous event or a different venue.

For each open item, record the question, the responsible contact and the decision needed. For example, ask whether equipment can remain after service rather than writing collection later without approval.

Keep the confirmed brief separate from exploratory messages. A single final document makes the agreed instructions easier to identify without searching through unrelated menu and guest-list discussions.

## FAQ


**What is a catering venue-access brief?**

A catering venue-access brief records how food, equipment and staff enter, work within and leave an event venue. It covers the delivery route, facilities, timings, responsibilities and decision contacts.

**Is a location pin enough for a Dubai catering delivery?**

A location pin is not a complete catering delivery instruction. Add the agreed entrance, unloading point, internal route and contact for access problems.

**Who should confirm catering access at my venue?**

The venue should confirm its access conditions, and the caterer should confirm the proposed working arrangements. The organiser should keep the final agreed version and circulate changes.

**Do I need an access brief for drop-off catering?**

Drop-off catering still needs clear delivery and handover instructions. Confirm who will receive the food, where it should go and which responsibilities remain with the host.

**Should serving staff and cleanup be included in the brief?**

Serving staff and cleanup responsibilities should be recorded explicitly. Specify the agreed service tasks, areas to be cleaned, rubbish arrangements and equipment collection rather than assuming they are included.

**What should I send myCHEF with a venue-access enquiry?**

Send myCHEF the event date, location, guest count, service required and any venue instructions already confirmed. Include the venue contact and identify access or equipment questions that remain unresolved.


## One last check: can everything leave?

Read the brief backwards before sending it. Start with equipment collection, rubbish removal and the final handover, then work back to service and arrival.

This catches a different set of questions from planning the entrance alone. In particular, confirm whether the agreed exit route remains accessible after guests leave and who will be present to complete the handover.

## Related guides

- [Serving staff and cleanup for Dubai catering](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-catering-companies-in-dubai-provide-serving-staff-and-cleanup)
- [Connecting office facilities management to lunch catering](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/how-to-connect-office-facilities-management-to-lunch-catering)

To discuss your event with myCHEF, send the **date, location, guest count and service required**, together with the venue-access brief. Identify anything still awaiting venue approval so the catering discussion starts with clear responsibilities.
